fullDescription:
The tunnel network that decided how the war in the south was fought, an hour and a half northwest of Ho Chi Minh City.

Cu Chi is around 250 kilometres of hand-dug tunnels on three levels, begun against the French in the 1940s and extended through the American war until it reached from the Cambodian border to the edge of Saigon. Whole villages lived underground: kitchens that vented smoke hundreds of metres away through disguised outlets, field hospitals, sleeping quarters, wells and workshops that turned unexploded ordnance into new weapons.

A section is opened for visitors and part of it has been widened, because the original dimensions are around 80cm high and 60cm wide and almost nobody from outside Vietnam fits. You can go in, and how far you go is entirely your choice; there are exit points every twenty metres or so for people who decide once they are down there that this is enough.

The trapdoors are the detail that stays with people. A hatch the size of a book tray, covered in leaf litter, vanishes completely once it is closed, and the guides demonstrate it with someone standing a metre away.

Going in the afternoon usually means fewer coaches than the morning slot, if you have a choice.

Pickup covers hotels in Districts 1, 3 and 4, with drop-off in District 1, in an air-conditioned bus or a minivan on the small-group option.

We book with Kim Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final.

Six and a half hours. Wear clothes you can crawl in. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Around 250km of hand-dug tunnels on three levels
Go inside a widened section, and stop whenever you want
Exit points every twenty metres if you change your mind
Trapdoor demonstration that disappears from a metre away
Afternoon slot usually has fewer coaches than the morning

fullDescription:
Three rides above the Muong Hoa valley in one afternoon, all of them looking out over the rice terraces.

Paragliding from Sapa is the one people remember. You launch from a ridge above the valley and fly tandem over terraced fields that climb the hillsides in steps, with Fansipan, the highest mountain in Indochina, on the skyline. The terraces change completely through the year: flooded and mirroring the sky around May and June, deep green through summer, gold just before the September harvest.

The alpine coaster is a gravity sled on rails through the hillside forest, and you control your own brake, so it is as fast or as gentle as you want it. The rainbow slide is the short, silly one, and it is the reason this works with teenagers who would not otherwise get on a paragliding flight.

Cat Cat Village sits in the valley below, a Hmong settlement a short walk down from Sapa town with a waterfall at the bottom.

Private transport and hotel pickup mean the three activities run back to back rather than with waits between them, which is what fits them all into four hours.

Paragliding depends on the air. Wind and low cloud ground flights, and Sapa sits high enough that the weather turns quickly, so the flight moves rather than launching in poor conditions.

We book with Ethnic Community Tours directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers hotel pickup and drop-off, private transport, the rainbow slide, the alpine coaster ride and the paragliding activity.

Four hours. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Tandem flight over the terraced Muong Hoa valley
Fansipan, the highest mountain in Indochina, on the skyline
Alpine coaster with your own brake: fast or gentle
Terraces mirror the sky in June and turn gold before harvest
Private transport, so all three run back to back

fullDescription:
Sapa's four best-known stops in a single day, including the summit of Indochina's highest mountain.

Fansipan is 3,143 metres and the cable car does it in around fifteen minutes, which used to be a two-day trek. The car crosses the Muong Hoa valley on the way up and the terraces open out beneath you; at the top there is a summit complex of temples and a final flight of steps to the marker. Cloud sits on the peak often enough that the view is genuinely luck, and locals will tell you mornings are the better bet.

Cat Cat is the Hmong village below Sapa town, walked down into rather than driven to, with a waterfall at the bottom and workshops where indigo dyeing and hemp weaving are still done.

Moana Sapa is the built one: a hillside of viewing platforms and installations made for photographs, with the valley as the backdrop. It is unapologetically a photo stop and it is very good at being that.

The alpine coaster is a gravity sled on rails through the forest, with your own brake.

All four tickets are included, which matters here: Fansipan's cable car, Cat Cat, Moana and the coaster each charge separately and the entry fees are a substantial part of a Sapa day.

We book with SST Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers Sapa town hotel pickup and drop-off, an English-speaking guide, transport, and tickets for Cat Cat Village, Moana Sapa, Fansipan and the coaster.

Eight hours. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Fansipan, 3,143m, by cable car in about fifteen minutes
Cat Cat Hmong village, indigo dyeing and a waterfall
Moana Sapa's viewing platforms above the valley
Alpine coaster through the forest with your own brake
All four entry tickets included, not paid gate by gate

fullDescription:
Ninh Binh's three headline sites in one day from Hanoi, with the boat trip that most itineraries get wrong.

Trang An is the one to insist on. It is the UNESCO-listed complex, and the two-hour rowing route passes through nine water caves cut straight through the limestone, some low enough that everyone ducks. It is quieter and longer than Tam Coc, the more commonly sold alternative, and the caves are the reason: at Tam Coc there are three, here there are nine. The rowers work the oars with their feet, which is a Ninh Binh thing you will not see elsewhere.

Mua Cave is the climb. Around 500 stone steps up to a dragon on the ridge, and from the top the Trang An river bends through the karst below you. It is the photograph that put Ninh Binh on the map.

Bai Dinh is the largest Buddhist complex in Vietnam: a corridor of 500 arhat statues, a 36-tonne bronze Buddha, and a scale that only registers when you realise the walk between halls is measured in kilometres. Electric buggies run inside for a reason.

Twelve hours covers the two-hour drive each way from Hanoi plus all three sites without rushing any of them.

Hotel transfer is within one kilometre of the Hanoi Opera House, excluding Hong Ha Road, so check your hotel falls inside that.

We book with SST Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers hotel transfer, transport and an English-speaking guide.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Trang An: nine water caves, against Tam Coc's three
Rowers work the oars with their feet
Mua Cave: around 500 steps to the ridge dragon
Bai Dinh, Vietnam's largest Buddhist complex, 500 arhat statues
Transfer covers hotels within 1km of the Hanoi Opera House

fullDescription:
Two hours learning Hmong batik in Ta Van village, using the tool and the dye the technique has always used.

Batik here is wax-resist drawing. You work molten beeswax onto hemp cloth with a chan, a small copper-tipped pen that holds the wax at temperature, then the cloth goes into an indigo vat. The dye takes everywhere the wax is not, and when the wax is boiled out the drawing appears white against blue. Hmong women learn the patterns from their mothers and each design carries meaning: spirals, snail shells, elephant feet, all of them carrying a story.

The indigo is the part that surprises people. The vat is a living fermentation, fed and kept alive over weeks, and cloth comes out of it green and turns blue in the air as it oxidises in front of you.

Ta Van sits in the Muong Hoa valley below Sapa, a Giay and Hmong village along the river, and the workshop runs in the village rather than in a town studio.

You take home what you make. Two hours is enough for a small piece done properly rather than a large one done badly.

All materials are included: beeswax, the chan tool and access to the indigo vat.

This runs whatever the weather, which in Sapa matters more than most places. Cloud and rain close the valley views and cancel the paragliding for much of the year; this does not move.

We book with Ethnic Community Tours directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final.

Two hours. Wear something you do not mind marking with indigo. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Hmong wax-resist batik with the traditional chan tool
A living indigo vat: cloth comes out green and turns blue
Patterns carry meaning, learned mother to daughter
Held in Ta Van village, not a town studio
Runs in any weather, when Sapa's views and flights do not

fullDescription:
A bicycle out to Tra Que, the herb village that supplies Hoi An's kitchens, with farming and a cooking class attached.

Tra Que is three kilometres from Hoi An's old town and has been growing herbs on the same ground for around 300 years. What makes it distinctive is the fertiliser: the farmers use algae dredged from the neighbouring lagoon rather than manure, which is why the basil, mint and coriander here have a reputation among Vietnamese cooks that ordinary market herbs do not.

You farm before you cook. That means the real work: turning soil with a two-headed hoe, raking beds, and watering with two cans hung from a shoulder pole, which is harder than the farmers make it look and is the part everyone remembers.

The cooking follows, using what you just picked.

The ride out is flat the whole way along the river, so it needs no fitness, and the bikes are collected from and returned to your hotel in the Hoi An area.

Option 2 adds a basket boat: the round woven coracle that Vietnamese fishermen use in the coconut palms, which spins rather than steers and is its own event.

Entrance tickets and an English-speaking guide are included.

We book with Hiep Hoi An Travel directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers hotel pickup and return by bicycle within the Hoi An area, entrance tickets, the guide, and the basket boat on option 2.

Around four and a half hours. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Tra Que: 300 years of herbs grown with lagoon algae, not manure
Real farm work: two-headed hoe, beds, shoulder-pole watering
Cook with what you picked
Flat riverside ride, no fitness needed
Option 2 adds a spinning basket boat in the coconut palms
